title: Container With Most Water
description:
# Container With Most Water

You are given an integer array `height` of length `n`. The value `height[i]` is the height of a vertical line whose x-coordinate is `i`.

Choose two different indices `i` and `j` with `i < j`. Together with the x-axis, those two vertical lines form a container. The amount of water held by that container is `(j - i) * min(height[i], height[j])`.

Return the maximum amount of water any such container can hold.

**Notice** that you may not slant the container. Only the shorter of the two chosen lines limits the water height.

## Example 1:

**Input:** height = [1,8,6,2,5,4,8,3,7]
**Output:** 49
**Explanation:** Choosing indices 1 and 8 gives width 7 and limiting height 7, so the area is 49.

## Example 2:

**Input:** height = [1,1]
**Output:** 1
**Explanation:** The only possible pair has width 1 and limiting height 1.

## Constraints:

*   `n == height.length`
*   `2 <= n <= 10^5`
*   `0 <= height[i] <= 10^4`

tests.description: Best width beats the taller adjacent pair
Zeros can appear between useful walls
Interior tall walls beat far lower endpoints
A very tall wall still needs enough width

solutions.name: Two Pointers - Elimination Proof
solutions.description:
## Approach

Place one pointer at each end of the array. Each step computes the area of the current pair, then moves the pointer at the shorter wall inward.

## Key Insight

If the left wall is no taller than the right wall, keeping the left wall while moving the right wall inward only reduces width and cannot increase the limiting height above `height[left]`. Every container using that left wall with a smaller width is therefore dominated, so the left wall can be discarded. The symmetric argument applies when the right wall is shorter.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Two Pointers with Dominated-Height Skips
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use the same two-pointer invariant, but after evaluating a pair, skip over consecutive walls that are no taller than the wall just discarded.

## Key Insight

Once the width has become smaller, a wall with height less than or equal to the discarded limiting wall cannot produce a larger area. Skipping those dominated walls is not a different proof; it is the same elimination argument made more aggressive in the implementation.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Descending Height Threshold Sweep
solutions.description:
## Approach

Sort indices by height from tallest to shortest. Sweep height thresholds downward. After all indices at the current height have been activated, the best container whose limiting height is at least that threshold uses the leftmost and rightmost active indices.

## Key Insight

For any optimal pair, when the shorter endpoint's height is processed, both endpoints are active. The farthest active span is at least as wide as that pair, so `currentHeight * (maxIndex - minIndex)` will consider an area at least as large as the optimal pair's area at that height threshold. This gives an offline sorting view of the same max-area problem.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n log n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Brute Force Pair Enumeration
solutions.description:
## Approach

Enumerate every pair of indices `i < j`, compute `(j - i) * min(height[i], height[j])`, and keep the largest value.

## Key Insight

This is the problem definition written directly as code. It is too slow for the full constraints, but it is the simplest correctness baseline and makes it clear what the optimized approaches are allowed to discard.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(1)
